metadata.name: file
metadata.description: Determine file type by examining file contents

installation.note: file is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The file command determines the type of a file by examining its contents rather than relying on the filename extension. It uses magic numbers and file signatures to identify file types, making it more reliable than checking extensions.
when_to_use: Identify file types when extensions are missing or incorrect
Check if a file is binary or text

syntax.description: Examine one or more files and display their types. Can also examine directories.

options.description: Do not prepend filenames to output lines (brief mode)
options.use_case: When you only want the file type without the filename, useful in scripts

options.use_case: To get MIME types for web applications or content-type headers

options.description: Follow symbolic links and examine the files they point to
options.use_case: To check the type of the target file, not the symlink itself

options.use_case: To examine device files and special filesystems

options.use_case: To identify the contents of compressed files without extracting them

misconceptions.title: file uses filename extensions
misconceptions.misconception: file determines file type by looking at the filename extension (.txt, .jpg, etc.)
misconceptions.reality: file examines the actual file contents using magic numbers and file signatures. It ignores filename extensions completely.
misconceptions.tip: You can rename a .txt file to .jpg and file will still correctly identify it as text, not an image

misconceptions.title: file only works on regular files
misconceptions.misconception: file can only examine regular files, not directories or special files
misconceptions.reality: file can examine directories (shows 'directory'), symbolic links, device files (with -s), and other special files.
misconceptions.tip: Use file on directories to confirm they're directories, or use -s for device files

common_pitfalls.description: Some binary files may be identified as generic 'data' if file doesn't recognize the format
common_pitfalls.solution: This is normal for some proprietary formats. Use -i to get MIME type, or check file headers manually with hexdump

common_pitfalls.description: By default, file shows the type of the symlink itself, not the target file
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -L flag to follow symbolic links and examine the target file type

best_practices: Use -b for scripting to get clean output without filenames
Use -i for web applications that need MIME types
Combine with find to check types of multiple files: find . -type f -exec file {} \;
Use -L when working with symbolic links to check target file types
Remember that file examines contents, not extensions - it's more reliable than checking .txt, .jpg, etc.
performance_tips: file is fast for single files but can be slow when checking many files
For batch operations, consider using find with -exec file for better performance
The -z flag adds overhead when examining compressed files

additional_notes.magic_numbers: file uses 'magic numbers' - specific byte sequences at the start of files that identify their type
additional_notes.mime_database: file uses a magic database (usually /usr/share/misc/magic) to identify file types
additional_notes.reliability: More reliable than filename extensions because it examines actual file contents
additional_notes.scripting: The -b flag is essential for parsing file output in scripts
